desc:
There are n junctions labelled 0 to n - 1. Each roads[i] = [a, b, w] is a two-way road of length w.

The eccentricity of a junction is the length of the shortest route to the junction that is farthest from it (measured by shortest route length). The radius of the network is the smallest eccentricity over all junctions, and the diameter is the largest one.

Return [radius, diameter]. If some junction cannot reach another, the eccentricities are undefined and you must return [-1, -1]. A network with a single junction has radius and diameter 0.

Example: n = 4, roads [[0,1,2],[1,2,3],[2,3,4]] (a path). Eccentricities are 9, 7, 5, 9 (for example junction 2 is 5 away from junction 0, 3 from junction 1 and 4 from junction 3), so the answer is [5, 9].
constraints: roads[i] = [a, b, w] with 0 ≤ a, b < n, a ≠ b and 1 ≤ w ≤ 1,000
No two roads join the same pair of junctions
hints: Eccentricity needs the shortest distance from a junction to all others. You need it for every junction.
Compute all-pairs shortest distances with Floyd-Warshall (n is only 80). Then the eccentricity of i is the maximum of row i.

If any entry of the matrix is still infinite, return [-1, -1]. Otherwise radius = min over rows of the row maximum, and diameter = max over rows of the row maximum (equivalently the largest entry in the whole matrix).
editorial: Build the shortest-distance matrix with Floyd-Warshall in O(n<sup>3</sup>). Row i of that matrix lists the distances from junction i, so its largest value is the eccentricity of i. The radius is the smallest of these row maxima and the diameter is the largest.

Disconnected networks are detected for free: some matrix entry is never improved from infinity. Note that the diameter is the length of the longest shortest route, not the longest simple path. Repeated Dijkstra also works in O(n · E log n); on a tree each eccentricity can even be found with two BFS passes, but the general weighted case needs one of the all-pairs approaches.
